title: Are Facial Expressions Universal?
objective: After this level you can explain Paul Ekman's evidence for universal expressions and the current debate over it.
summary: Ekman's 1971 study with the Fore suggested some facial expressions are universal. Lisa Feldman Barrett argues they vary far more than that, and the debate continues.

cards.headline: A photo of a face, shown to people with little outside contact.
cards.body: In 1971, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen took photographs of faces to the Fore people of Papua New Guinea and asked a simple question: which face goes with this story? If people everywhere pick the same face, are expressions built in?

cards.headline: Ekman's case for universals
cards.body: Ekman and Friesen told short emotional stories and asked the Fore to choose the matching photographed face. Tasks like this, in small societies with little outside contact, gave strong evidence that people everywhere recognize the same expressions. Ekman's side adds that congenitally blind people, who never saw a face, move their faces much as sighted people do. Ekman's side lists seven: happiness, surprise, sadness, fear, disgust, contempt and anger.

cards.headline: Barrett's challenge
cards.body: In 2019, Lisa Feldman Barrett led a review that pushed back. Yes, people smile when happy and scowl when angry more often than chance. But how people express emotions varies a lot across cultures, situations and people. Most studies had people pick from a short list, which makes contrary evidence hard to find. Asked to name faces freely, people in small societies rarely gave the expected words. Trobriand Islanders read the wide-eyed gasp that Western studies call fear as a threat.

cards.headline: A debate still open
cards.body: Barrett proposes that emotions are constructed from experience, so one bodily state can become different emotions in different situations. The other side keeps finding support too: in 2021, Jessica Tracy's team reported that the Mayangna of Nicaragua recognized bodily expressions of anger, sadness and fear above chance. Both sides agree faces carry a lot of information. The argument is over how fixed and universal it is.

cards.headline: Faces: debated
learned: Ekman: the Fore matched faces to stories
Ekman's side: blind people move their faces much like sighted people
Barrett: expressions vary with culture and situation
Tracy: bodily expressions recognized in Nicaragua

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or group with their part in the facial expression debate.
questions.explanation: Ekman and Friesen tested the Fore people. Barrett proposes emotions are constructed from experience. Jessica Tracy's team studied the Mayangna of Nicaragua, and Trobriand Islanders read the wide-eyed gasp as a threat.

questions.prompt: Why does Barrett's review say matching tasks like Ekman's may overstate universality?

options.label: Picking from a short list makes contrary evidence hard to find
The photos used in them were too blurry to read
options.rationale: Image quality was not the criticism.

options.label: Only blind people took part in the tests
options.rationale: Blind expressers were a separate line of evidence.

options.label: The stories were told in the wrong language
options.rationale: The review criticized the answer format.

questions.explanation: When people choose from a short list, agreement looks high; asked to name faces freely, people in small societies rarely gave the expected words.

questions.prompt: Barrett argues one bodily state can become different emotions in different situations. Which Level 45 theory made a similar claim?

options.label: The James-Lange theory
options.rationale: James-Lange ties each feeling to its own arousal pattern.

options.label: Drive theory
options.rationale: Drive theory explains motivation, not emotion.

options.label: The Cannon-Bard theory
options.rationale: Cannon-Bard says arousal and feeling run on separate tracks.

questions.explanation: The two-factor theory says arousal gets its emotional label from the situation, much like Barrett's constructed emotions.
